The card maps each repeated (source, target) id pair to its edge count: (2, 3) has 3, (1, 2) has 2." width="100%"} Returns a dictionary showing how many edges exist between each pair of nodes that has multiple edges. Only includes pairs with 2 or more edges. For undirected graphs, returns unordered pairs (smaller node ID first). Multiple (parallel) edges are common when a graph is built from event or transaction data: several emails between the same two people, several flights on the same route, repeated co-authorships. This method summarizes that multiplicity, which helps you: - check whether a graph is a multigraph before running algorithms that assume simple graphs - decide how to collapse repeated edges, for example into a single edge whose weight is the count - find the node pairs with the strongest repeated interaction For directed graphs, `A -> B` and `B -> A` are different pairs, so two edges in opposite directions are not counted as multiple edges. Repeated self-loops on a node appear as the pair `(node, node)`. Use `which_multiple()` to get the individual edge IDs instead of counts, and `simplify()` to remove duplicates (and self-loops) altogether. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[tuple[int, int], int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Dictionary mapping `(source_id, target_id)` to edge count, sorted by pair. Only includes pairs with count `>= 2`; an empty dictionary means the graph has no multiple edges. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Aggregates the same information `which_multiple()` reports as a per-pair tally: for every endpoint pair with at least two edges, the entry $(u, v) \mapsto k$ records the exact multiplicity. Undirected graphs canonicalize each pair so the smaller node ID comes first, which lets client code index directly without worrying about orientation. Self-loops are included only when a node carries two or more of them, matching the multiplicity threshold used for ordinary pairs. A single pass over the edges makes this $O(E)$. Useful for planning edge consolidations, weighted rollups, or multigraph-to-weighted-graph conversions. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Rather than listing every duplicated edge, this groups them by node pair and reports how many edges connect each pair: ::: {#7ef672c5 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(directed=True) g.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) g.add_edges( [ ("A", "B"), ("A", "B"), # Duplicate ("A", "B"), # Another duplicate ("B", "C"), ("B", "C"), # Duplicate ] ) counts = g.count_multiple() # Convert to labels for a readable summary { (g.get_label_from_id(src), g.get_label_from_id(tgt)): count for (src, tgt), count in counts.items() } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {('A', 'B'): 3, ('B', 'C'): 2} ``` ::: ::: In a directed graph, edges running in opposite directions are not duplicates of each other. Adding `C -> B` leaves the `(B, C)` count unchanged and creates no new entry: ::: {#525150fa .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} g.add_edge(source="C", target="B") len(g.count_multiple()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: This is useful for planning which edges to consolidate, such as merging repeated shipping routes between the same two cities into a single weighted edge: ::: {#9eb37d4d .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} transport = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["CityA", "CityB", "CityC"]) .add_edges( [ ("CityA", "CityB", {"route": "highway"}), ("CityA", "CityB", {"route": "railway"}), ("CityA", "CityB", {"route": "airline"}), ("CityB", "CityC", {"route": "highway"}), ] ) ) # Returns {('CityA', 'CityB'): 3} -- 3 routes to consolidate { (transport.get_label_from_id(id1), transport.get_label_from_id(id2)): count for (id1, id2), count in transport.count_multiple().items() } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` {('CityA', 'CityB'): 3} ``` ::: :::
